title: He Made *The Coffin in the Mountain*, the Best Chinese Thriller in Years, to Show Audiences There Is No Absolute Good or Bad
excerpt: Xin Yukun says *The Coffin in the Mountain* is a film for cinephiles.
body:
Xin Yukun says *The Coffin in the Mountain* is a film for cinephiles.

For most moviegoers, last weekend's cinemas belonged to Marvel's *Ant-Man*, the animated *The Little Prince*, or *Goodbye Mr. Loser*. But a small number of people, by design or by accident, saw a domestic film called *The Coffin in the Mountain* and came out thrilled.

It is a suspense drama set in rural Henan. An unidentified corpse turns up and is claimed, one after another, by three different families. The absurd "change of ownership" of a coffin drags all three households into its wake... It sounds like yet another brainless domestic movie, except that this time the story is remarkably complete and gripping.

Those who have seen it have not held back their praise. *The Coffin in the Mountain* has an 8.5 rating on Douban. The last mainland Chinese film to score higher was Jiang Wen's *Let the Bullets Fly*, in 2010. On the film's Douban page, some call it "the biggest surprise among domestic films this year," and others bring up Nolan, the Coen brothers, Quentin Tarantino, Korean genre films...

The name Xin Yukun is as unfamiliar as the film. *The Coffin in the Mountain* is the 31-year-old director's first feature. He says its greatest strength is the story: "That's the foundation of genre film, but because everyone does it so badly, when a good one comes along, people like it." But he also says the price of a 1.7 million yuan budget and a 24-day shoot is that "apart from the story, every element loses points": the acting, the cinematography and the staging could all have been better.

We interviewed him the day before the film opened, when he was busy with promotional screenings. Despite the good reviews, the film got only about 3% of screenings on its opening weekend. As for the box office, Xin says he just hopes the distributor does not lose money, though even that will be hard. As of the 19th, the film had grossed 4.7 million yuan. In the director's words, this is a film for cinephiles: it has few commercial elements, a rural setting, and above all no stars at all. The actors he found locally in Henan aren't even good-looking.

Among cinephiles, the real star this film has made is the director himself. Xin brings to mind Cao Baoping, director of *The Dead End*, who also sticks doggedly to genre film and has also won critical praise without commercial success. In fact, Cao Baoping was the one who discovered Xin Yukun. As a juror at the 2014 FIRST Film Festival, he insisted on giving Xin both of the top prizes, Best Film and Best Director.

We talked with the young director about how the film was made, the state of today's film market, and his own career plans.

![Director Xin Yukun](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607175245HMlyaRdONimvzZ85.jpg-w600)

**The plot, where a coffin passes among three families, is reportedly a true story?**

Yes. I met my producer, Ren Jiangzhou, when I was making my short film *Seven Nights*. At the end of 2011 he told me a story. His mother had come from the Henan countryside to visit him. Because he worked in film, he took her to a movie, *Love Is Not Blind*, telling her it had made several hundred million at the box office. Afterwards she said, what's so interesting about that, it's just two people falling in love, let me tell you a story. And she told him about something that had happened back in their hometown in Henan.

I was very interested. But at the time I hadn't worked out how to write it, and the money wasn't certain either. In early 2013 the producer said he could find a small sum and we could shoot it. I had been looking for a chance to make a feature, so I started writing the script and preparing.

**How long did the script take? Were there disagreements while you were writing it?**

I started in early 2013 and was still revising when shooting began at the end of 2013, so a little under a year. At first there was a lot of disagreement over the script. I wrote three versions. One was linear, another had a different theme altogether, and the third is the multi-threaded narrative you see now. We settled on the third, and after that the writing went smoothly.

**What was the theme of the other version?**

The producer and I disagreed at the time. He thought a film on such a small budget could never get a theatrical release. If we were aiming for film festivals, the third version's narrative was very complicated and its design was so obvious; should we switch to a theme that exposed more of reality? It would put more weight on the era: the wave of migrant labor, country people who leave and never come back, and why they don't.

**But you didn't like a more "lofty" theme like that?**

To be honest, none of us much liked it. What I loved most was the coffin changing hands among three families. We all grew up watching genre films, and we felt a film should be more fun and should give the audience something concrete to hold on to. Besides, even if we had shot it around that theme, there was no guarantee the festivals would like it. No one can say. In the end we chose the version we felt most passionate about, the one that most fired our creativity.

**The film's title reportedly changed three times. Why?**

The first draft of my script was called *Heart Matters*, two characters that are very interesting in Chinese. Nobody goes around every day with an empty head, grinning blankly. Some people carry deep worries, involving very big secrets. I found that interesting.

When we submitted *Heart Matters* for review, we found the title was already taken, and we were going to change it to *The Coffin Burial*. But that seemed to position the film wrongly. Audiences would wonder whether we were discussing survival, or earth burial. The distributor felt it would push away many viewers, since a coffin is a bit unlucky. They were right, so we came up with *The Coffin in the Mountain* (the Chinese title, 《心迷宫》, means "maze of the heart"). A maze gives the audience a god's-eye view of ordinary people. The characters have no idea what is happening to them. Only the audience knows.

**On funding: this was your debut, and although the story has popular appeal, the setting is rural. Did many film companies turn you down?**

Not a cent of the film's money came from the industry (the budget was 1.7 million yuan). For one thing, we had no professional resources or connections. My producer said he was confident in 2013 because a friend of his in business offered to help and give us the money. Looking at it today, if we had kept banging our heads against people who invest in films, the film might still not have been made.

For another, as you said, the subject matter has limits: it is a rural story. Investors might read the first ten pages and lose interest. So in hindsight, staying away from the industry was the right call.

So we simply put our heads down and did it ourselves. The upside was that nobody was going to restrict our freedom much.

**It was your first film. Where did you find the actors and crew?**

The actors are professionals from Henan: from local theater companies and song-and-dance troupes, and bit-part actors from local TV dramas.

Once the script was finished I was sure it was an ensemble piece, with heavy main roles that are hard to play. I decided from the start that we had to use professional actors, but on a limited budget we couldn't hire familiar faces from TV dramas, only experienced local actors.

The most important member of the core team was my production manager, who assembled much of the crew for me. The cinematographer is a very good friend of mine who shoots commercials. He had always wanted to shoot a feature and was thrilled at the chance to work together.

**How long was the shoot?**

From the first day of shooting to wrap took 26 days, of which 24 were working days.

We stopped for two days. One was because an actor wasn't working out and had to be replaced. The other was because the money hadn't arrived. It hadn't arrived before shooting began either; the producer was out looking for money the whole time and wasn't with the crew after we started. He was worried that without money in the account he couldn't pay wages, so we stopped for a day to rest and wait, and then the money gradually came in.

**Shooting a film of nearly two hours in 24 days is an astonishing pace.**

It comes mostly from my experience shooting TV series. Also, the film wasn't difficult to shoot: lots of dialogue and mood scenes, no big set pieces. We shot more per day than a TV drama does. A TV drama does three script pages a day; we did four or five.

We were also afraid of running out of money and leaving the film unfinished, so we didn't polish things much during the shoot. If a scene was a bit off, I didn't fuss over it and moved on. I never thought about settling down and doing it properly. All I thought was that it must not die halfway.

![A still from The Coffin in the Mountain](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606071752461X2pWxcbglGVUnJ0.jpg-w600)

**On style: the film looks much like a documentary, yet strong drama emerges. The camera is handheld throughout, with no fixed positions. What was your thinking?**

This is actually a strongly plot-driven film, which should be shot the classic way, cutting between big close-ups and wide shots to build tension. But we had the cinematographer shoot with the camera on his shoulder, which saves a lot of money. With a moving camera, the audience's eye rests on the characters, because the audience itself is constantly moving. With a traditional fixed camera, the audience notices the sets, and you need plenty of money for art direction.

We also wanted to give the audience something different: it looks like news footage, everyone talks in a flat, unremarkable way, yet the plot is highly dramatic. That contrast is interesting.

Before shooting, my key visual crew, the art director, cinematographer and lighting, and I watched documentary-style films like *A Separation* and *Winter's Bone*.

**Many viewers' comments online mention the Coen brothers, Nolan, Tarantino.**

As a viewer, these are the directors I love most. They all have a strong personal stamp and are fun, so audiences enjoy watching them.

People need something highly recognizable to talk about. With Nolan it's the narrative structure, which is very convoluted. With the Coens and Tarantino, none of the characters they create is purely good. The Coen brothers like to film ordinary people, good people, who do bad things at the critical moment.

**Speaking of which, how do you explain the film's "twisted values," a worldview in which everyone is a bad person?**

That really is my view of filmmaking and of the world: in life there is no absolute black and white, no absolute good and bad. We each see life from a different angle, and a man guilty of monstrous crimes may be a devoted son at home. In many Western films, human nature is portrayed truthfully. We have seen so many films with lofty, upright characters that when we see a film like this, we feel, well, a bit uncomfortable.

![A still from The Coffin in the Mountain](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607175246K81Wjbn9tYgHoqJp.jpg-w600)

**Many people are praising the film now, but you have said it doesn't show you at your best?**

Overall it would probably score just a pass. As I see it, every element was losing points, and only the story was left. In the market at large, story is the foundation of commercial and genre films, but it is usually told badly. So this film is bad at everything except the story, and because the story is good, people think the film is good.

**Looking back, do you have any regrets?**

Because of the budget and my own inexperience, the cinematography, the staging and the actors could all have been better. Many viewers, especially those in the front rows, said, wow, your camera is too shaky, it makes me dizzy. It was my first time working for the big screen, and I shot it as if for the small screen.

The story is probably as good as it was going to get. Everything else could have been better, especially the actors.

**You mentioned that at the start the producer hadn't even thought of a theatrical release?**

Back then, a theatrical release for this film would have been a fantasy. It had such a low budget, no stars, and we couldn't even be sure we would finish shooting.

My own private motive was that, as a film student, I needed a debut feature to take this step. If I could finish it, I'd be satisfied. I didn't think much about where it would go from there. My producer said that if it really didn't work and came out too poor, we could cut it into a three-episode legal-affairs TV series and sell it to a TV station to recoup the money. If it turned out decent, we could sell it to video websites or the like.

Then it went to film festivals. At the end of last year Taihe Entertainment came on board and wanted to give it a wide release.

**What are your box-office expectations?**

Just not to lose money. I don't want the distributor to lose any more. The film's cost is low, so I'm not asking for much.

**Are you worried about how ordinary audiences will react?**

I'm nervous. This is a film with a cinephile temperament. It has no stars and no commercial elements. I worry that people won't get through the first ten minutes.

I also worry the marketing will mislead people. Expectations can sometimes ruin a film. Some viewers saw the poster and said they expected big set pieces. I thought, oh no, there are no big set pieces at all.

During the promotional screenings I slowly gained confidence. Audiences responded very well, and they read the film the way I meant it. Maybe I had underestimated them.

![A still from The Coffin in the Mountain](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607175247T8dhCZOwxafNQoql.jpg-w600)

**Let's talk about how you became a director. I heard you dropped out of high school to study film?**

I dropped out in my second year of high school. A friend studying in Xi'an said a school there was recruiting for a film program. My grades were poor, and getting into university was going to be a problem anyway, so I talked it over with my family and said I wanted to study this.

It went very badly. You're supposed to finish high school properly, take the exams for the Beijing Film Academy or the Central Academy of Drama, and only after graduating can you hope to work in this field. I didn't know that, so I fell into a trap. After a year at that school I felt it was a very poor school with a mediocre curriculum. I came back to take the Film Academy exam, failed, and started shooting TV series in Xi'an for television stations and the like. Then in 2008 I came to the Beijing Film Academy for further study. So I was stuck in a trough the whole time, and around 30 I wanted to prove something to myself, and give up if it didn't work.

**Now that *The Coffin in the Mountain* is finished, do you feel different?**

The difference was last year, when I first started going to festivals and was excited. I had been held down for a year and a half, and at last, at last, I could lift my head. That was when I went to Venice and Busan, festivals I love.

This year I've calmed down. I've also realized that getting into the industry doesn't mean everything goes smoothly and opportunities pile up. Working with better funders and better filmmakers is a step up, but the problems you face on that step are not simpler. They are more complicated.

**Have many film projects come your way?**

Yes, ever since the FIRST festival last year, but none has been a fit. Most of what film companies bring me is IP, an established story, perhaps set in ancient times or an invented world. First, the cost would be huge, and second, I'm not very interested.

**Do you mean something like *Ghost Blows Out the Light*?**

That one I would be interested in. But it's very hard to shoot.

**What is your next film? Do you have specific plans?**

I've already shot *Distance*, produced by Anthony Chen. It's a film by three directors, due out early next year. Its theme is emotional bonds: family, friendship and love. I shot the family segment, starring Chen Bolin.

**Will it be very different from *The Coffin in the Mountain*?**

Yes. People who see it will think, my god, did the same person make these? I really like Anthony Chen's *Ilo Ilo*, and this time I also went to learn from him.

![A still from The Coffin in the Mountain](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607175247892FoULJG6QvqaN5.jpg-w600)

**And your own next feature? What will it be like?**

My next feature is at the script stage, and it will have crime, suspense and action elements. The story will be designed for a mass audience. I haven't thought much about casting yet.

In features, I'm committed to genre film. Many good genre films carry the director's strong personal style. Big companies operate entirely with the market and the audience in mind. I will make films for the market too, but I hope to keep my personal style.

At this stage I'm still not really suited to very mainstream commercial films. For now I want to make films that engage with real society, like *Saving Mr. Wu*: documentary-style genre films with commercial packaging.
